newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - High flying BTPs to stay airborne.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - High flying BTPs to stay airborne.

text.p: Investors in Italian bonds may be suffering a touch of vertigo after the market's recent dizzying performance but analysts said on Thursday they should close their eyes and keep their nerve.

A short-term correction was likely but only a complete derailment of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would spark a sharp widening of the Italian/German yield gap. And even then, the damage would not be too severe.
Investors worried about EMU should stick to the short-to-medium-end of the yield curve where economic fundamentals would still allow outperformance.

"I'm waiting for a correction in the Italian market," said Kim Thomsen, head of fixed income at Danske Invest in Copenhagen, which has $1.2 billion invested in fixed income. "If we go to 140 basis points short term, this could be a buying opportunity."
At 1200 GMT, the 10-year BTP/Bund yield spread was quoted at 121 basis points, a new record low and well below a recent peak of 155 on June 9.
The market has been steaming ahead since the conclusion of the Amsterdam summit when Germany and France put EMU back on track with a deal to make employment part of the process.
"It seems to me if we are going towards monetary union -- and everything is pointing in that direction -- then we could see the spread narrow even further from here," Thomsen said.
He had a target of 100 basis points by the end of the year if EMU keeps chugging along and a spread of 50 if Italy secures a place in the first round.

"The risk is of course that Italy is not going to be a member of monetary union at the first stage. The spread could easily see 150 basis points but I don't think it's going to be much more than that because fundamentals are in the right place," Thomsen said.
Indeed good news on the economic front has been an additional boon to BTPs recently.
Italy was likely to post a state sector surplus of nearly 30 trillion lire for June, allowing the overall deficit to come near the 3.0 percent of GDP target required by EMU, analysts said.
Preliminary inflation for June from 11 sample cities on Friday were expected to show inflation running at a tame 1.4-1.6 percent year-on-year.
Two sticking points were welfare talks where Prime Minister Romano Prodi will be hard pressed to push through reforms and the Bank of Italy's reticence on interest rate cuts.

"They don't want the lira to move rapidly in the other direction. They're very aware of the fragility of the currency," said Rob Stewart, investment manager at funds group Matheson Investment Ltd in London.
Stewart said the Italian yield curve was already pricing in rate cuts. Two-year notes were currently yielding 6.159 percent compared with a discount rate of 6.75 percent in Italy.
But he expected rate cuts to eventually come through and the curve to steepen further.
"My positioning at the moment is in the three-to-five-year sector," he said.

Ernesto Rameriez, European economist at Bankers Trust in London was more pessimistic on Italy longer term. The harsh steps Italy has taken to meet the EMU criteria were unlikely to be repeated in 1998.
"At the end of the day the argument will be on sustainability and that still leaves Italy looking like an ugly duckling," he said.
